paragraphs: A data market must make two connected decisions: which providers’ data to spend a customer’s training budget on, and how to divide the resulting revenue among those providers. Assessing each provider’s contribution separately can be expensive. The paper addresses both decisions together through an algorithm that the authors describe as running in linear time.

The central mechanism is adaptive sampling. As training proceeds, the algorithm accesses providers whose data contribute more to the model more frequently. Those access frequencies also determine compensation. This connects purchasing and payment through the same process: data that prove more useful receive both more attention during training and greater compensation.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for efficient budget use and revenue allocation with properties similar to those associated with Shapley values. This is a similarity in allocation properties, rather than a claim that the algorithm computes identical payments. The method supports centralized and federated settings, and an empirical evaluation examines practical scenarios and baseline comparisons. Together, these contributions offer a computationally practical approach to coordinating data acquisition and contributor rewards.
icml-2023-addressing-budget-allocation-a.tldr: An adaptive sampling algorithm jointly allocates training budgets and provider payments by accessing and compensating more useful data providers more often.

paragraphs: Transformers commonly build depth by repeatedly alternating attention and feed-forward layers. This paper investigates whether that uniform arrangement is the most efficient choice. Its finding is that more complicated blocks, with different arrangements of familiar layer types, can improve both model quality and computational efficiency.

The resulting Brainformer block combines sparsely gated and dense feed-forward layers with attention, alongside different normalization and activation choices. The contribution concerns how these components are organized within the network. A more varied architecture can therefore be worthwhile even though its block design is less simple than the usual repeating pattern.

In the reported comparison, a Brainformer with eight billion activated parameters per token achieves twice as fast training convergence and five times faster step time than its GLaM counterpart. It also obtains a 3% higher SuperGLUE score after fine-tuning than GLaM with a similar activated parameter count. Few-shot evaluations additionally favor Brainformer over a searched Primer dense model with similar computation per token. These results support the paper’s claim that architectural complexity can purchase useful efficiency gains.
icml-2023-brainformers-trading-simplicit.tldr: Brainformer rearranges diverse Transformer components into more complex blocks that improve quality and efficiency in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Continual learning can cause a neural network to lose previously acquired knowledge as tasks or domains change. Replaying stored examples throughout training can reduce this forgetting, but incurs repeated computation. This paper examines whether forgetting is spread evenly across the network, using metrics that track the training behavior of individual modules.

The analysis identifies a small set of modules that are especially task-specific and sensitive to changes, while other modules retain more shareable knowledge. The proposed Forgetting Prioritized Finetuning, or FPF, updates only the sensitive modules using a small stored buffer after continual learning. Targeting relatively few parameters makes this corrective step computationally efficient.

A second method, k-FPF, replaces replay at every training step with a limited number of periodically triggered FPF updates. Across the evaluated class- and domain-incremental benchmarks, FPF substantially improves existing methods, while k-FPF maintains comparable accuracy with lower computational cost. The authors also examine buffer size, training epochs, and module selection. The findings support concentrating replay-based correction on the parts of a network most affected by task changes.
icml-2023-does-continual-learning-equall.tldr: Targeted fine-tuning of modules most sensitive to task changes reduces forgetting and can replace costly continual replay in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Adversarial noise can cause a neural network to make incorrect predictions, and denoising models are one way to defend against it. However, the paper notes that denoisers can fail or even have negative effects when an attacker has full knowledge of the defense. It therefore changes how denoising is approached.

The method first discards information using complementary masks. The purpose is to disrupt the spatial structure of adversarial noise while retaining robust information about the underlying sample. Guided denoising models then reconstruct representations useful for reliable prediction from the masked inputs. The two stages combine deliberate disruption with selective restoration.

This design focuses on preserving robust predictive features rather than only learning a direct transformation from an attacked sample into a natural-looking sample. Experiments report competitive performance against white-box attacks and show that the approach reverses the negative effects of denoising models in the tested settings. The contribution is an empirically supported defense strategy in which removing some information can help a restoration model recover the information that matters for prediction.
icml-2023-eliminating-adversarial-noise-.tldr: Complementary masking followed by guided representation restoration provides competitive defense against the white-box attacks evaluated in the paper.

paragraphs: Generating descriptions of medical images requires connecting complex visual findings with appropriate medical terms. This paper addresses that challenge when labeled training data are limited. Its framework uses uncertainty estimates to decide where human feedback would be informative and then incorporates that feedback into both caption generation and later training.

The interaction begins with a list of predicted keywords, each accompanied by evidence-based uncertainty. The system selects informative keywords for user feedback, then conditions caption generation on the approved keywords. This gives users a way to influence the content of a description through intermediate terms rather than relying only on the initially generated caption.

The final stage retrains the model using user-approved keywords and captions, with uncertainty determining how different training examples are weighted. Human input therefore serves two purposes: guiding the current description and improving subsequent predictions. Experiments on two medical image datasets show that the framework can learn effectively from feedback and improve future captioning performance. These are findings about captioning and interactive learning, while the abstract presents reduced physician workload and fewer medical errors as potential motivations.
icml-2023-evidential-interactive-learnin.tldr: An interactive medical captioning framework uses uncertainty to request keyword feedback, guide captions, and improve the model through retraining.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples through a process described by differential equations, but emulating that process can require hundreds or thousands of network evaluations. This paper targets that sampling cost by learning the relationship between an initial noise sample and the reverse diffusion trajectory. The aim is to produce images with a single model evaluation.

The proposed method, diffusion model sampling with neural operator, or DSNO, uses a neural operator to map a Gaussian initial condition to a continuous-time solution trajectory. It adds temporal convolution layers to a diffusion backbone, with those layers parameterized in Fourier space. Their role is to represent relationships across time along the trajectory.

Learning the trajectory in this form enables parallel decoding, whereas other fast sampling approaches discussed in the abstract remain sequential. In the one-model-evaluation setting, the authors report state-of-the-art FID values of 3.78 on CIFAR-10 and 7.83 on ImageNet-64. The result demonstrates that trajectory-level learning can deliver competitive image generation under an especially tight sampling budget, with the reported quality claims specifically tied to that single-evaluation setting.
icml-2023-fast-sampling-of-diffusion-mod.tldr: DSNO learns reverse diffusion trajectories with a neural operator, enabling parallel image generation in one model forward pass.

paragraphs: A graph can tend to connect nodes from the same class or nodes from different classes. The paper argues that training only on the observed graph can overlook useful structure associated with the opposite tendency. For a graph dominated by same-class connections, that missing information concerns different-class relationships, and the reverse applies to graphs dominated by different-class connections.

Graph cOmplementAry Learning, or GOAL, addresses this through two components. Graph complementation first identifies the missing kind of structural information and constructs a complemented collection containing both connection tendencies. A specially designed graph convolution then processes this richer structure. The convolution is developed from an optimization perspective.

The approach changes both the structural information supplied to a graph neural network and the way that information is processed. Its motivation is that the dominant pattern in an observed graph need not provide all useful relationships for learning. On eight real-world datasets, GOAL consistently outperforms all evaluated baselines. Those experiments support combining complementary connection structures across the graph settings studied.
icml-2023-finding-the-missing-half-graph.tldr: GOAL augments graphs with complementary same-class and different-class connection structure and learns from both using a tailored convolution.

paragraphs: Image restoration can benefit from modeling relationships across an entire image, but existing global approaches often consume substantial memory and overlook the particular degradation being corrected. Fourmer develops a more efficient way to model this global information. Its design draws on two properties of the Fourier representation of images.

First, Fourier transforms can separate degradation from image content to some extent, providing useful prior information about the restoration problem. Second, each location in Fourier space involves information from all spatial pixels, making global interactions inherent to the representation. The separation claim is partial: the motivation does not require degradation and content to become perfectly isolated.

Fourmer retains a design organized around spatial interaction and channel evolution, but implements both through customized Fourier-based components. The authors report competitive performance on image de-raining, enhancement, dehazing, and guided super-resolution while using fewer computational resources. These results suggest that Fourier-domain structure can support useful global restoration without the resource demands of the global modeling approaches considered in the paper.
icml-2023-fourmer-an-efficient-global-mo.tldr: Fourmer uses Fourier-based spatial and channel modeling to achieve competitive image restoration with fewer computational resources.

paragraphs: A model can fit its training data perfectly yet still predict well on new data, a phenomenon called benign overfitting. This paper studies that behavior in sparse linear regression, where the true coefficient vector has relatively few nonzero entries and observations contain additive noise. The question is what makes a particular exact fit generalize well.

One explanation is implicit regularization: the training procedure favors certain solutions without an explicit penalty selecting them. Such preferences are often described through minimum-norm solutions. However, the authors show that neither the minimum l1-norm nor the minimum l2-norm interpolator attains optimal test loss for the sparse regression problem considered.

The paper introduces a different model parameterization whose gradient-descent dynamics combine benefits associated with those two interpolators. The analysis establishes that training reaches an exact fit with near-optimal test loss. This provides a concrete example in which the route taken during optimization matters for generalization, and the resulting implicit preference goes beyond ordinary norm minimization. The theoretical contribution concerns this sparse linear regression construction.
icml-2023-implicit-regularization-leads-.tldr: A new sparse linear regression parameterization lets gradient descent find an exact training fit with near-optimal test loss through implicit regularization.

paragraphs: The probability flow ordinary differential equation associated with a diffusion model supports deterministic inference and exact likelihood evaluation. Nevertheless, the paper observes that diffusion ODEs have lagged behind leading likelihood-based generative models on likelihood performance. It addresses that gap through changes to both training and evaluation.

For training, the authors introduce velocity parameterization and investigate variance reduction to speed convergence. They also derive a higher-order flow-matching objective with an error bound for fine-tuning. This objective improves ODE likelihood and makes the trajectory smoother, connecting the training criterion with the behavior of the continuous transformation used by the model.

For evaluation, the paper introduces truncated-normal dequantization that requires no additional training and addresses a mismatch between training and evaluation. Combining the proposed techniques yields reported state-of-the-art likelihood results on image datasets, including 2.56 on CIFAR-10 and 3.43/3.69 on ImageNet-32. These results are achieved without variational dequantization or data augmentation. The contribution is a coordinated set of training and evaluation improvements for diffusion ODE likelihood modeling.
icml-2023-improved-techniques-for-maximu.tldr: Improved training objectives, parameterization, and evaluation dequantization strengthen diffusion ODE likelihood results on image datasets.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, several agents must improve their policies toward a shared objective. Policy optimization with function approximation is widely used, but establishing statistical guarantees is difficult. This paper investigates when individual agents can make local policy updates that collectively reach a globally optimal policy.

The analysis uses a multi-agent performance difference lemma to characterize the optimization landscape. It identifies a localized action-value function as an appropriate descent direction for each agent’s policy. Based on that observation, the authors construct a multi-agent version of proximal policy optimization in which each agent updates its own policy similarly to standard PPO.

The global convergence result holds under standard regularity conditions on the Markov game and conditions involving problem-dependent quantities, with a sublinear convergence rate. It is therefore a conditional guarantee for the analyzed setting. The authors also extend the algorithm to off-policy learning and introduce pessimism into policy evaluation, reporting alignment with experiments. The main contribution is a provably convergent PPO approach for cooperative Markov games that connects local updates to a global objective.
icml-2023-local-optimization-achieves-gl.tldr: A multi-agent PPO algorithm achieves sublinear convergence to a globally optimal policy under the paper’s regularity and problem-dependent conditions.

paragraphs: The paper studies fair allocation when indivisible items arrive one at a time in an arbitrary order. Agents have additive, normalized valuations, and the authors treat desirable goods and burdensome chores separately. Fairness is assessed through approximations to maximin share allocations, with competitive guarantees describing what online algorithms can achieve.

When all agents value items identically, these problems connect to established machine covering and load balancing settings. The paper instead allows agents to have different additive valuations. For goods, this changes the possibilities sharply: no competitive algorithm exists even with three agents, while the authors provide an optimal 0.5-competitive algorithm for two agents.

For chores, the paper gives a (2 − 1/n)-competitive algorithm for at least three agents and a square-root-of-two competitive algorithm for two agents. It also proves that no two-agent algorithm can improve beyond a competitive factor of 15/11. The two-agent chore bounds therefore leave a gap between the achieved factor and the impossibility threshold. The results distinguish both goods from chores and two-agent allocation from larger groups.
icml-2023-multi-agent-online-scheduling-.tldr: The paper establishes algorithms and impossibility bounds for online maximin-share allocation, with sharply different results for goods and chores.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a trained model to changing test data without access to its original training data. Many approaches focus on changes in the input distribution. This paper studies a broader setting in which both the inputs and the distribution of labels change, so adaptation must address two sources of mismatch together.

The authors call this problem test-time adaptation with Open-world Data Shift. They first analyze how classification error relates to distribution shifts, then use that analysis to motivate ODS. The framework separates the mixed shift into covariate and label components and handles each accordingly. This makes the distinction between the two kinds of change part of the adaptation procedure.

Experiments cover multiple benchmarks and different shift types, with ODS outperforming the state-of-the-art methods included in the comparisons. The authors also state that the framework is suitable for many test-time adaptation algorithms. Its contribution is thus both a problem formulation that explicitly includes changing label distributions and a broadly applicable framework for addressing that change alongside shifts in the inputs.
icml-2023-ods-test-time-adaptation-in-th.tldr: ODS separates input and label distribution shifts so test-time adaptation can address both without revisiting source data.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated interaction between two cooperative players who act in sequence. In each round, a leader chooses an action, and a follower responds after observing it. The leader learns from past interactions and seeks to minimize cumulative regret, so the central question concerns how much experience is needed to make effective decisions.

The distinguishing assumption is that the follower knows the true reward completely and always chooses a best response to the leader’s action. Although the players cooperate, this informed response does not produce a uniformly simple learning problem for the leader. The structure of the reward determines how the follower’s behavior affects learning difficulty.

The authors show that sample complexity can vary from constant to exponential depending on that reward structure, even for linear cooperative Stackelberg games. The result makes the follower’s knowledge and response rule central to the analysis. It shows why studying the leader as an ordinary learner without accounting for the responding player can miss substantial differences in the difficulty of regret minimization.
icml-2023-online-learning-in-stackelberg.tldr: An omniscient best-responding follower can make the leader’s learning complexity range from constant to exponential, depending on the reward structure.

paragraphs: Online generalized linear regression makes predictions over successive rounds while learning from noisy labels. This paper considers labels generated by a generalized linear model with additive stochastic noise that may be unbounded. It develops a sharper analysis of follow-the-regularized-leader, or FTRL, to describe how noise affects accumulated regret.

For sigma-sub-Gaussian label noise, the regret upper bound is O(sigma² d log T) plus a term that grows more slowly than log T. Here, d is the input dimension and T is the number of rounds. A lower bound of order sigma² d log(T/d) for stochastic online linear regression shows that the upper bound is nearly optimal.

The analysis also extends to a more refined Bernstein noise condition. As an application, the authors study generalized linear bandits with heterogeneous noise and design an FTRL-based algorithm with a variance-aware regret bound. This connects the regression analysis to sequential action selection, where accounting for differences in noise levels can yield a more informative performance guarantee than treating all observations as equally noisy.
icml-2023-optimal-online-generalized-lin.tldr: A sharper FTRL analysis gives nearly optimal noise-dependent regression regret and enables a variance-aware guarantee for generalized linear bandits.

paragraphs: Programmers often begin a complicated implementation with its control-flow outline and add details progressively. ChainCoder brings a related structure to Python program generation. Instead of predicting the complete program in one pass, the model generates it through multiple passes organized from coarse structure to finer components.

The method uses abstract syntax tree parsing to separate source code into layout frames and accessory components. These form a hierarchical representation that determines the prediction objective: each pass produces a subsequence, and the subsequences are assembled according to the hierarchy. A tailored Transformer jointly encodes the natural-language specification and syntactically aligned input-output examples.

The hierarchy gives the generation process explicit intermediate structure, connecting the order of prediction to the organization of a program. Extensive evaluations report that ChainCoder outperforms the state-of-the-art systems compared in the paper. The authors interpret these results as evidence that progressive generation makes the reasoning procedure easier and guides the model toward better solutions. The contribution is a synthesis system whose code representation, training objective, and architecture all support outline-first generation.
icml-2023-outline-then-details-syntactic.tldr: ChainCoder generates Python programs through syntax-guided passes that build an outline before filling in details.

paragraphs: An accessible language-generation API can supply examples for training another model through distillation. This paper addresses how a model owner could detect that a suspect model was derived from the protected system. Existing watermarks based on word choices or synonym replacement can be defeated by countermeasures such as randomizing synonyms.

GINSW embeds secret signals into the token probability vectors used during decoding. The owner then probes a suspect model and looks for the corresponding secret message. The method therefore aims to leave a detectable signature of the protected model’s generation behavior that can be checked after a possible extraction attempt.

Experiments show effective identification of distilled suspect models while minimally affecting the protected API’s generation quality. Under the evaluated watermark-removal attacks, GINSW improves detection mean average precision by an absolute 19 to 29 points over previous methods. These findings support stronger detection in the tested adversarial conditions. The practical protection described here comes from tracing a model’s origin through its watermark, rather than a demonstrated guarantee that distillation itself cannot occur.
icml-2023-protecting-language-generation.tldr: GINSW embeds secret signals in decoding probabilities to identify distilled models, improving detection under evaluated watermark-removal attacks.

paragraphs: Linear evaluation freezes a pretrained model and trains a separate classifier on its features. Logistic regression is a common default, but this paper asks whether naive Bayes can offer better statistical efficiency. It revisits the comparison between generative and discriminative classifiers in the context of modern pretrained representations.

The theoretical analysis extends classical binary results to multiple classes and works with surrogate losses. Under mild assumptions, multiclass naive Bayes needs O(log n) samples to approach its asymptotic error, whereas the corresponding logistic regression needs O(n), with n denoting feature dimension. This compares how quickly each reaches its own limiting error, so it does not establish that naive Bayes always has the better final error.

The authors develop a multiclass H-consistency framework and an explicit logistic-loss bound to support the analysis. Gaussian-mixture simulations validate the theoretical pattern, and experiments with pretrained vision models show faster convergence for naive Bayes as data increase. Results also suggest promise in few-shot learning and reveal a two-regime pattern for supervised pretrained models. The work makes classifier choice an explicit part of transfer learning design.
icml-2023-revisiting-discriminative-vs-g.tldr: Theory and experiments show that naive Bayes can approach its limiting error with fewer samples than logistic regression on pretrained features.

paragraphs: In pure-exploration bandit problems, sampling serves to identify a good option for eventual use. Simple regret measures how far the selected option’s mean reward falls below the best. This paper improves guarantees for that criterion both when the sampling budget is at least the number of options and when there are too few samples to inspect every option.

The central result is a sharper, instance-dependent analysis of Sequential Halving. It bounds the probability of selecting an option more than epsilon below the best for every positive epsilon, even though the algorithm does not take epsilon as an input. The analysis yields a worst-case simple regret rate of square root of n/T, optimal up to logarithmic factors.

The bound also essentially matches an existing instance-dependent lower bound for identifying an epsilon-good option. For the data-poor setting, the authors introduce Bracketing Sequential Halving, which obtains the same improvement without requiring every option to be sampled. Experiments on real-world tasks show this variant outperforming the compared methods. The contribution combines stronger guarantees for a familiar algorithm with a variant designed for limited sampling budgets.
icml-2023-revisiting-simple-regret-fast-.tldr: Sharper Sequential Halving analysis and a bracketing variant improve guarantees for selecting a good bandit arm, including when samples are scarce.

paragraphs: Vision-language models learn representations that connect images with text, typically using large training collections. RLEG explores whether generative diffusion models can supply additional training material directly in representation space. Its augmentation operates on feature embeddings, the numerical representations produced by image and text encoders.

The method first extracts embeddings for both modalities. Pretrained diffusion-based generators then transfer embeddings between the visual and language domains during training. The generated embeddings become additional samples for contrastive learning within a modified CLIP framework. Generation is therefore integrated into representation learning as an ongoing source of augmented feature-level examples.

This approach uses the generative capacity of diffusion models to strengthen another model’s representation learning process. The authors report effective representations and state-of-the-art results across image classification, image-text retrieval, object detection, semantic segmentation, and text-conditioned image generation. The breadth of the evaluated tasks suggests that the learned features are useful for several kinds of visual and multimodal prediction. The stated findings support embedding generation as a practical augmentation mechanism for vision-language learning.
icml-2023-rleg-vision-language-represent.tldr: RLEG generates cross-modal feature embeddings with diffusion models and uses them as training augmentations for vision-language representation learning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning often assumes that recorded trajectories include states, actions, and rewards. This paper studies a mixed-data setting: some trajectories contain all three, while others record states and rewards but omit actions. The goal is to use both collections to train an agent without requiring every trajectory to have action labels.

The proposed pipeline first learns an inverse dynamics model from the fully labeled trajectories. That model supplies proxy action labels for the action-free trajectories. An offline reinforcement learning algorithm then trains on the combined true-labeled and proxy-labeled data. The pipeline is designed as a general wrapper that can work with different offline learning algorithms.

On several D4RL benchmarks, certain algorithms match versions trained with fully labeled data even when only 10% of trajectories have action labels and those labeled trajectories are highly suboptimal. The result is specific to the reported algorithm and dataset combinations. A larger controlled study examines how data properties and choices of inverse dynamics and offline learning method interact, identifying trends and practices for making this semi-supervised approach effective.
icml-2023-semi-supervised-offline-reinfo.tldr: Learning proxy action labels from a small labeled trajectory set lets offline reinforcement learning use additional action-free experience.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems often combine dynamics learning, planning, policy learning, value estimation, and auxiliary objectives to improve sample efficiency. This paper investigates how much of that complexity is needed for useful representation learning. It finds that a latent dynamics model trained through temporal consistency alone can provide representations sufficient for strong performance in the evaluated settings.

The learned representation supports two uses. A planning system can use a dynamics model conditioned on it to choose actions, or a model-free learner can use it as input features for its policy and value function. The same representation-learning idea therefore applies both to systems that plan explicitly and to those that act without planning.

For challenging high-dimensional locomotion tasks, the planning version learns accurate dynamics while training 4.1 times faster than ensemble-based methods. In model-free experiments, especially Humanoid and Dog tasks, the approach substantially outperforms compared model-free methods and matches model-based sample efficiency while training 2.4 times faster. These results support temporal consistency as a sufficient representation-learning signal for the tested tasks, with benefits in both data use and computation.
icml-2023-simplified-temporal-consistenc.tldr: Representations learned through latent temporal consistency support strong planning and model-free reinforcement learning with faster training in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Protein language models acquire information from large collections of natural protein sequences. LM-Design adapts that sequence knowledge to a structural design task: proposing protein sequences for a given fold. The paper’s central idea is to add structural awareness to an existing sequence model so that both sources of information guide generation.

The method inserts a lightweight structural adapter into the protein language model. During inference, iterative refinement further optimizes the proposed sequences. This provides a generic way to reprogram sequence-based models for structure-conditioned design while drawing on the evolutionary information already learned from natural sequences.

Experiments report sequence-recovery accuracy gains of 4% to 12%, including 55.65% and 56.63% on the CATH 4.2 and 4.3 single-chain benchmarks and above 60% for protein complexes. Additional analyses show that the approach uses structural and sequential knowledge in structurally non-deterministic regions, benefits from larger datasets and models, and generalizes to examples including antibodies and de novo proteins. The reported findings establish stronger sequence design and recovery performance across the studied settings.
icml-2023-structure-informed-language-mo.tldr: LM-Design adds a structural adapter and iterative refinement to protein language models, improving sequence design for specified folds.

paragraphs: Filling missing entries in a dataset requires learning enough about the underlying distribution to supply plausible values. This paper uses the premise that two incomplete batches drawn from the same dataset originate from the same distribution. Their completed versions should therefore be compatible at the distribution level.

The method sends both batches through deep invertible transformations into a latent space and matches their distributions there. It learns the transformations and the missing values together through a joint algorithm. The transformed representation supplies the space in which consistency between batches guides imputation, linking the proposed values to a shared distribution rather than treating missing entries independently.

The authors report that the algorithm requires fewer hyperparameters to tune and produces high-quality imputations across different mechanisms for generating missingness. Extensive comparisons across many datasets and benchmark methods yield reported state-of-the-art performance. These findings support transformed distribution matching as an effective way to use incomplete samples collectively. The same-distribution premise is central to the approach: it explains why agreement between batches provides useful information for learning their missing values.
icml-2023-transformed-distribution-match.tldr: The method jointly learns missing values and invertible transformations by matching incomplete batches’ distributions in a latent space.

paragraphs: Copy-Paste augmentation creates segmentation training examples by placing object instances onto different backgrounds. Its usefulness depends on having diverse, high-quality objects to paste, but obtaining them from manual annotations or rendered 3D models can be costly. X-Paste addresses this acquisition bottleneck so the augmentation strategy can operate at greater scale.

The framework obtains category-specific images in two ways: generating them with text-to-image models such as StableDiffusion, or filtering noisy web-collected images with zero-shot recognition models such as CLIP. A data acquisition and processing pipeline makes these sources usable for Copy-Paste, and the paper systematically studies the resulting approach.

On LVIS, X-Paste improves a CenterNet2 baseline with a Swin-L backbone by 2.6 box AP and 2.1 mask AP across all categories. Gains are larger for long-tail categories, reaching 6.8 box AP and 6.5 mask AP. These results demonstrate the feasibility of expanding the supply of augmentation objects through generation and filtering. They also show particularly strong benefits for the less common categories in the reported evaluation.
icml-2023-x-paste-revisiting-scalable-co.tldr: X-Paste scales Copy-Paste augmentation using generated and automatically filtered object images, with especially large reported gains on long-tail categories.
